# IPv4
su **estructura** es llamada notacion decimal punteada y es representada por 4 numeros decimales entre 0 y 255.

con IPv4 una mascara de subnet tambien es necesaria. *Una mascara de subnet* es un valor de 32-bits que diferencia la porcion de red de la porcion de host. Esta unida a la direccion IPv4 y determina de que subnet el dispositivo es miembro

por ejemplo en la direccion 192.168.1.10, subnet mask (255.255.255.0), el default gateway (192.168.1.1) asignado a un host. El *default gateway* es la direccion IP de el router que el host va a usar para acceder a redes remotas por default que el host va a usar para acceder a reddes remotas por default 

campos del header IPv4
![[Pasted image 20260425173858.png]]
- **Version:** indica que el paquete es IPv4. Usa 4 bits y su valor es **0100**.
- **Differentiated Services or DiffServ(DS)** campo de 8 bits usado para definir la prioridad del paquete. Incluye los bits **DSCP**, para clasificación de servicio, y **ECN**, para notificación de congestión.
- **Header checksum** sirve para detectar errores o corrupción en el encabezado IPv4.
- **Time to Live / TTL:** limita el tiempo de vida del paquete. Cada router reduce este valor en 1. Si llega a 0, el paquete se descarta y se envía un mensaje **ICMP Time Exceeded** al origen.
- **Protocol:** identifica el protocolo de nivel superior que transporta el paquete, por ejemplo **ICMP = 1**, **TCP = 6** o **UDP = 17**.
- **Source IPv4 address:** contiene la dirección IPv4 del dispositivo que envía el paquete. Siempre es una dirección **unicast**.
- **Destination IPv4 address:** contiene la dirección IPv4 del receptor del paquete. Puede ser **unicast**, **multicast** o **broadcast**.
los dos mas importantes son origen y destino, tipicamente no cambian en el viaje de origen a destino.
el Internet Header Length (IHL), total length y header checksum son usados para identidficar y validar el paquete

otros campos del encabezado IPv4 ayudan a gestionar la fragmentación de paquetes. Los campos **Identification**, **Flags** y **Fragment Offset** se usan para rastrear y reordenar fragmentos cuando un paquete se divide. Esto puede ocurrir cuando un router reenvía un paquete a una red con una MTU más pequeña.

Los campos **Options** y **Padding** rara vez se usan y no se cubren en este módulo.
#### limitaciones de IPv4
- **Agotamiento de direcciones IPv4:** IPv4 cuenta con un número limitado de direcciones públicas únicas disponibles. Aunque existen aproximadamente 4 mil millones de direcciones IPv4, el creciente número de nuevos dispositivos con conexión a Internet, las conexiones permanentes y el crecimiento potencial de las regiones menos desarrolladas han incrementado la necesidad de más direcciones.
- **Falta de conectividad de extremo a extremo:** la traducción de direcciones de red (NAT) es una tecnología que se implementa comúnmente en las redes IPv4. NAT ofrece una forma de que múltiples dispositivos compartan una sola dirección IPv4 pública. Sin embargo, debido a que la dirección IPv4 pública es compartida, la dirección IPv4 de un host de la red interna queda oculta. Esto puede ser problemático para las tecnologías que requieren conectividad de extremo a extremo.
- **Mayor complejidad de la red:** aunque el NAT ha prolongado la vida útil de IPv4, solo estaba pensado como un mecanismo de transición a IPv6. El NAT, en sus diversas implementaciones, añade complejidad a la red, lo que genera latencia y dificulta la resolución de problemas.

# IPv6
las direcciones IPv6 son de 128 bits de longitud y son escritas como una string de valores hexadecimales. Cada 4 bits son representados por 1 digito hexadecimal, por un total de 32 valores hexadecimales. por ejemplo: 2001:db8:acad:10::10.

mejoras respecto a IPv4:
- mas espacio de direccionamiento
- mejora en manejo de paquetes: con menos campos header
- elimina la necesidad de usar NAT

campos principales del header IPv6
- **Version:** indica que el paquete es IPv6. Usa 4 bits y su valor es **0110**.
- **Traffic Class:** campo de 8 bits equivalente al campo **Differentiated Services (DS)** de IPv4. Se usa para clasificar o priorizar paquetes.
- **Flow Label:** campo de 20 bits que permite que los routers den el mismo tratamiento a todos los paquetes que pertenecen al mismo flujo.
- **Payload Length:** campo de 16 bits que indica la longitud de los datos o payload del paquete IPv6. No incluye el encabezado IPv6, que tiene un tamaño fijo de **40 bytes**.
- **Next Header:** campo de 8 bits equivalente al campo **Protocol** de IPv4. Indica qué tipo de datos transporta el paquete para entregarlos al protocolo de capa superior correcto.
- **Hop Limit:** reemplaza al campo **TTL** de IPv4. Cada router reduce este valor en 1. Si llega a 0, el paquete se descarta y se envía un mensaje **ICMPv6 Time Exceeded** al host de origen. En IPv6 no existe **Header Checksum**, por lo que los routers no necesitan recalcularlo, mejorando el rendimiento.
- **Source IPv6 Address:** campo de 128 bits que identifica la dirección IPv6 del host que envía el paquete.
- **Destination IPv6 Address:** campo de 128 bits que identifica la dirección IPv6 del host que recibe el paquete.
algun paquete IPv6 puede llegar a contener extension headers (**EH**) que proveen informacion opcional de capa de red. Estan ubicados entre el header IPv6 y el payload y son usados para fragmentacion, seguridad, para soporte de mobilidad y mas.

a diferencia de IPv4, los routers no fragmentan paquetes IPv6

# como routea un host
el source host debe ser capaz de enviar el paquete a host de destino.
otro rol de el network layer es como dirigir paquetes entre hosts.

un host puede enviar un paquete a los siguientes tipos de receptores:
- itself (a si mismo):
	- IPv4 direccion especial 127.0.0.1
	- IPv6 ::1, llamada loopback
- local host: es un host de destino que esta en la misma red que el host.
	- hosts de origen y destino comparten la misma direccion de red
- remote host: es un host en una red remota.
	- host de origen y destino no comparten la misma direccion de red
![[Pasted image 20260508152741.png]]
determinar si un paquete esta dirigido a un local host o a un remote host:
- IPv4: el dispositivo source usa su propia subnet junto a su direccion IPv4 y el destino IPv4 para determinarlo
- IPv6: el router local anuncia la direccion local de red (prefix) a todos los dispositivos en la red
en una red local, los dispositivos se conectan mediante un switch o punto de acceso inalámbrico y pueden comunicarse directamente si están en la misma red IP. Para comunicarse con dispositivos fuera de la red local, como en internet, se necesita un router. El router de la red local se llama **puerta de enlace predeterminada** y se encarga de buscar la mejor ruta hacia el destino.

# default gateway
es el dispositivo de red por default que puede routear trafico a otras redes. (es como una puerta al mundo exterior)
usualmente en una red, un default gateway es un router con estas features:
- tiene direccion IP local en el mismo rango que los otros hosts en la red local
- acepta trafico dentro de la red local y reenvida datos al exterior de la red local
- routea trafico a otras redes
sin default gateway no es posible reenviar trafico fuera de la red local.

### host routean a default gateway
una tabla de routeo tipicamente incluye un default gateway. 
En IPv4, el host recibe la direccion del default gateway de alguna de estas dos maneras:
- dinamicamente usando DHCP
- configurada manualmente
En IPv6, tambien se recibe la direccion de alguna de las dos maneras:
- el router anuncia el default gateway
- configurada manualmente

# introduccion al ruteo
cuando se envia un paquete y este llega a un router, este examina la direccion IP y analiza su tabla de ruteo para determinar donde reenviar el paquete.
la tabla de ruteo lista todas las direcciones de red conocidas (prefijos) y a donde hacer forwarding del paquete.
el router va a reenviar el paquete usando la mejor entrada (mas larga) de la tabla de ruteo.

ejemplo tabla de ruteo: ![[Pasted image 20260508154521.png]]

## tipos de entradas en una tabla de ruteo
La **tabla de enrutamiento** de un router contiene las rutas hacia las redes conocidas. Incluye tres tipos principales:
- **Redes directamente conectadas:** redes unidas a las interfaces activas del router.
- **Redes remotas:** redes alcanzables a través de otros routers, aprendidas manualmente o mediante protocolos de enrutamiento dinámico.
- **Ruta predeterminada:** se usa cuando no existe una ruta más específica hacia el destino; funciona como “último recurso”.

un router puede aprender acerca de redes remotas de cualquiera de estas 2 maneras:
- manualmente: son agregadas manualmente a la tabla de ruteo usando rutas estaticas
- dinamicamente: son agregadas automaticamente usando dynamic routing protocol

## ruteo estatico:
las rutas estaticas son entradas de rutas que son configuradas manualmente.
es suceptible a cambios en la topologia de red, porque implica volver a actualizar las entradas en la tabla de ruteo cuando surgen estos cambios.

ejemplo:
![[Pasted image 20260508155052.png]]
R1 es configurado manualmente con una ruta estatica para alcanzar la red 10.1.1.0/24.
si el camino hacia la red 10.1.1.0/24 cambia, sera necesario una nueva entrada en la tabla de ruteo de R1

##### caracteristicas:
- **Enrutamiento estático:** las rutas se configuran manualmente.
- **Cambios en la red:** si la topología cambia, el administrador debe modificar la ruta.
- **Uso recomendado:** redes pequeñas o con pocos enlaces redundantes.
- **Uso común:** se combina con un protocolo de enrutamiento dinámico para configurar una default gateway.

## ruteo dinamico
permite a los routers aprender acerca de redes remotas automaticamente, incluyendo tambien una ruta default por otros routers.
los routers que usan routeo dinamico comparten informacion con otros routers y no necesitaran modificarse por un administrador cuando hayan cambios en la topologia.

los protocolos de routeo dinamico incluyen OSPF y EIGRP
![[Pasted image 20260508155915.png]]

- **Enrutamiento dinámico:** el administrador solo debe habilitar las redes directamente conectadas.
- **Descubrimiento automático:** el protocolo encuentra redes remotas.
- **Actualización de rutas:** mantiene la información de enrutamiento actualizada.
- **Mejor ruta:** elige automáticamente el mejor camino hacia cada red.
- **Recuperación:** busca una nueva ruta si la actual deja de estar disponible.

# MAC & IP
### destino en misma red
a veces cuando un host debe mandar un mensaje, solo conoce la direccion IP del dispositivo de destino.
el host necesitara conocer la direccion MAC de ese dispositivo

hay 2 direcciones primarias asignadas a un dispositivo en un Ethernet LAN:
 - direccion fisica (MAC) : usada para comunicacion NIC to NIC en la misma red Ethernet
 - direccion logica (IP) : usada para enviar el paquete desde el dispositivo de origen hasta destino.

### destino en red remota
cuando la direccion IP (IPv4 o IPv6) de destino esta en una red remota, la direccion MAC de destino sera la direccion del default gateway. Ej.: la interface del router.

# ARP
si se esta usando IPv4, el Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) es lo que se necesita para mapear direcciones IPv4 a MAC.

todos los dispositivos en una red Ethernet tiene un Ethernet MAC unico. Cuando un dispositivo envia un frame Ethernet de capa 2, contiene estas 2 direcciones:
- direccion MAC de destino: es la direccion MAC del dispositivo en el mismo segmento de red. Si el host de destino esta en otra red, entonces la direccion MAC de destino sera el default gateway
- direccion MAC de origen: es la direccion MAC del Ethernet NIC del host de origen.

## funciones de ARP
- resolver direcciones IPv4 a direcciones MAC
- mantener una tabla de mapeo de direcciones IPv4 a direcciones MAC

cuando un paquete es enviado a la capa data link para ser encapsulado en un frame Ethernet, el dispositivo buscara la direccion de destino en su tabla ARP que este mapeada a la direccion IPv4. Esta tabla es guardada temporalmente en RAM.

- si la direccion IPv4 de destino esta en la misma red que el host origen, el dispositivo va a buscar por la direccion IPv4 en la tabla ARP.
- si la direccion IPv4 de destino esta en una red distinta que el host origen, el dispositivo va a buscar por la direccion IPv4 del default gateway en la tabla ARP.

hay 2 direcciones primarias asignadas a un dispositivo en un Ethernet LAN:

  • direccion fisica (MAC) : usada para comunicacion NIC to NIC en la misma red Ethernet
  • direccion logica (IP) : usada para enviar el paquete desde el dispositivo de origen hasta destino.

destino en red remota

ARP

si se esta usando IPv4, el Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) es lo que se necesita para mapear direcciones IPv4 a MAC.

todos los dispositivos en una red Ethernet tiene un Ethernet MAC unico. Cuando un dispositivo envia un frame Ethernet de capa 2, contiene estas 2 direcciones:

  • direccion MAC de destino: es la direccion MAC del dispositivo en el mismo segmento de red. Si el host de destino esta en otra red, entonces la direccion MAC de destino sera el default gateway
  • direccion MAC de origen: es la direccion MAC del Ethernet NIC del host de origen.

funciones de ARP

  • resolver direcciones IPv4 a direcciones MAC
  • mantener una tabla de mapeo de direcciones IPv4 a direcciones MAC

cuando un paquete es enviado a la capa data link para ser encapsulado en un frame Ethernet, el dispositivo buscara la direccion de destino en su tabla ARP que este mapeada a la direccion IPv4. Esta tabla es guardada temporalmente en RAM.

  • si la direccion IPv4 de destino esta en la misma red que el host origen, el dispositivo va a buscar por la direccion IPv4 en la tabla ARP.
  • si la direccion IPv4 de destino esta en una red distinta que el host origen, el dispositivo va a buscar por la direccion IPv4 del default gateway en la tabla ARP.

**CSMA/CA** (_Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance_) es el protocolo de control de acceso al medio utilizado fundamentalmente en redes inalámbricas (estándar IEEE 802.11 / Wi-Fi). A diferencia de la versión cableada (CD), este protocolo se centra en **evitar** la colisión antes de que ocurra, ya que en un medio inalámbrico es difícil o imposible detectar una colisión mientras se transmite.

### Desglose de componentes
1. **Carrier Sense (Detección de Portadora):** El dispositivo escucha el espectro de radiofrecuencia para verificar si el canal está libre antes de intentar transmitir.
2. **Multiple Access (Acceso Múltiple):** Múltiples dispositivos compiten por el uso del mismo canal de frecuencia.
3. **Collision Avoidance (Evitación de Colisiones):** En lugar de transmitir apenas el canal está libre, el protocolo introduce esperas aleatorias y confirmaciones para minimizar la probabilidad de choque.
    
### Funcionamiento del Algoritmo
El proceso sigue una lógica preventiva estricta:
1. **Escucha y Espera DIFS:** El nodo escucha el canal. Si está libre, debe esperar un tiempo fijo llamado **DIFS** (_Distributed Inter-Frame Space_).
2. **Backoff Aleatorio (Contienda):** Tras el tiempo DIFS, el nodo no transmite inmediatamente. Genera un número aleatorio de "slots" de tiempo (temporizador de backoff) y comienza una cuenta regresiva mientras el canal siga libre.
3. **Transmisión:** Cuando el temporizador llega a cero, el nodo envía la trama completa.
4. **Confirmación (ACK):** Dado que el emisor no puede escuchar colisiones mientras transmite, requiere una confirmación explícita.
    - El receptor, si recibe los datos sin errores (CRC correcto), espera un tiempo corto (**SIFS**) y envía un **ACK** (_Acknowledgement_).
    - **Si no llega el ACK:** El emisor asume que hubo una colisión o interferencia y repite el proceso (aumentando la ventana de backoff).
### Mecanismo Opcional: RTS/CTS
Para solucionar el problema del "nodo oculto" (nodos que no se escuchan entre sí pero colisionan en el punto de acceso), se puede usar un paso previo:
- **RTS (Request to Send):** El emisor pide permiso para transmitir.
- **CTS (Clear to Send):** El punto de acceso da "luz verde" y reserva el canal, silenciando a los demás nodos.

> **Nota técnica:** CSMA/CA es necesario porque las radios inalámbricas generalmente operan en **Half-Duplex** y la señal transmitida es mucho más potente que la recibida, lo que "ensordece" al dispositivo e impide detectar colisiones entrantes (Collision Detection) simultáneamente.

**CSMA/CD** (_Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection_) es un protocolo de control de acceso al medio utilizado en redes Ethernet para gestionar la transmisión de datos en un canal compartido. Su función principal es evitar la corrupción de datos cuando dos dispositivos intentan transmitir simultáneamente.

### Desglose de componentes
1. **Carrier Sense (Detección de Portadora):** Antes de transmitir, el dispositivo "escucha" el medio físico (cable). Si detecta voltaje (señal en curso), asume que el canal está ocupado y espera.
2. **Multiple Access (Acceso Múltiple):** Indica que múltiples nodos están conectados al mismo medio físico y compiten por su uso.
3. **Collision Detection (Detección de Colisiones):** El dispositivo monitorea el medio _mientras_ transmite. Si detecta una amplitud de onda superior a la propia (interferencia constructiva), identifica que ha ocurrido un choque de señales.
### Funcionamiento del Algoritmo
El proceso opera bajo la lógica "escuchar-transmitir-verificar":
1. **Monitoreo:** El nodo verifica si el canal está libre.
2. **Transmisión:** Si el canal está libre, comienza el envío de la trama.
3. **Verificación Continua:** Durante la transmisión, el nodo sigue escuchando.
    - **Si no hay colisión:** La transmisión finaliza con éxito.
    - **Si hay colisión:**
        1. Se detiene la transmisión de datos inmediatamente.
        2. Se envía una **Señal de Atasco (Jamming Signal)** de 32 bits para asegurar que todos los nodos en la red detecten la colisión.
        3. Se ejecuta el algoritmo de **Backoff Exponencial Binario**: el nodo espera un tiempo aleatorio antes de intentar transmitir nuevamente (para evitar que ambos nodos reintenten al mismo tiempo exacto).
> **Nota técnica:** CSMA/CD es exclusivo de redes **Half-Duplex** (como las basadas en Hubs o cable coaxial). En las redes modernas con Switches y operación **Full-Duplex**, las colisiones no ocurren, por lo que este protocolo no se utiliza.

## 📘 ¿Qué es un SFP?
- **SFP (Small Form-factor Pluggable)** es un **transceptor modular** que se inserta en switches, routers o firewalls.
- Convierte señales **eléctricas ↔ ópticas** (o eléctricas ↔ eléctricas) para permitir distintas formas de conexión.
- Es **hot-swappable**: se puede conectar o retirar sin apagar el equipo.

---
## 🔄 ¿Para qué sirve?
- Permite elegir **tipo de medio y velocidad** sin cambiar el equipo.
- Se usa para:
  - Enlaces de fibra óptica
  - Enlaces Ethernet de cobre
  - Conexiones de larga distancia
  - Interconexión entre switches (uplinks)

---

## 🧩 Componentes de un SFP
- **Láser o transmisor** (envía datos)
- **Receptor óptico** (recibe datos)
- **Interfaz eléctrica** hacia el switch/router
- **Conector de fibra o RJ-45** según el tipo

---

## 🔗 Tipos de SFP según el medio

### 🌈 SFP de Fibra Óptica
- Usan conectores **LC**
- Tipos comunes:
  - **SX** → fibra multimodo, corta distancia
  - **LX** → fibra monomodo, larga distancia
  - **ZX** → distancias muy largas

### 🔌 SFP de Cobre
- Conector **RJ-45**
- Usan cable UTP (Cat5e/Cat6)
- Alcance típico: hasta 100 m

---

## 🚀 Velocidades comunes

| Tipo | Velocidad |
|----|-----------|
| SFP | 1 Gbps |
| SFP+ | 10 Gbps |
| SFP28 | 25 Gbps |
| QSFP+ | 40 Gbps |
| QSFP28 | 100 Gbps |

> ⚠️ Un puerto SFP **no acepta SFP+**, pero un puerto SFP+ suele aceptar SFP.

---

## 📏 Alcance típico (fibra)

| Tipo | Fibra | Distancia |
|---|---|---|
| SX | Multimodo | hasta 550 m |
| LX | Monomodo | hasta 10 km |
| ZX | Monomodo | 40–80 km |

---

## 🔁 Full-Duplex
- Los SFP trabajan en **full-duplex**:
  - Transmiten y reciben datos al mismo tiempo
- Usan:
  - Dos fibras (Tx / Rx)
  - O una sola fibra (BiDi)

---

## 🧪 SFP BiDi (Bidireccional)
- Usa **una sola fibra**
- Transmite y recibe con **longitudes de onda distintas**
- Siempre se usan **en pares compatibles** (ej. 1310/1550 nm)

---

## ✅ Ventajas
- Modular y flexible
- Ahorra costos de hardware
- Ideal para uplinks y backbone
- Escalable (solo cambias el módulo)

---

## ❌ Desventajas
- Más caro que UTP
- Requiere compatibilidad (vendor lock-in)
- Fibra más delicada que cobre

---

## 📌 Puntos clave para CCNA
- SFP es **capa 1 (Física)**
- Diferenciar:
  - Fibra vs cobre
  - SX vs LX
  - SFP vs SFP+
- Saber cuándo usar SFP en lugar de UTP
- Muy común en enlaces **switch ↔ switch**

  • Escalable (solo cambias el módulo)

  • Más caro que UTP
  • Requiere compatibilidad (vendor lock-in)
  • Fibra más delicada que cobre

  • SFP es capa 1 (Física)
  • Diferenciar:
    • Fibra vs cobre
    • SX vs LX
    • SFP vs SFP+
  • Saber cuándo usar SFP en lugar de UTP
  • Muy común en enlaces switch ↔ switch

## 📘 ¿Qué es Auto MDI-X?
- **Auto MDI-X (Automatic Medium-Dependent Interface Crossover)** es una función que permite a un puerto Ethernet **detectar y ajustar automáticamente** los pines de transmisión (Tx) y recepción (Rx).
- Elimina la necesidad de elegir entre **cable directo (straight-through)** o **cruzado (crossover)**.

---

## 🔌 ¿Qué problema resuelve?
- En Ethernet tradicional:
  - Dispositivos **iguales** → cable crossover
  - Dispositivos **distintos** → cable straight-through
- Con **Auto MDI-X**:
  - 👉 **Cualquier cable funciona** (directo o cruzado)

---

## 🧠 ¿Cómo funciona?
- El puerto detecta automáticamente:
  - Qué pines se usan para transmitir
  - Qué pines se usan para recibir
- Si detecta que Tx/Rx no coinciden:
  - Los **invierte internamente** sin intervención del usuario

---

## 🖥️ Dispositivos que lo soportan
- Switches modernos
- Routers modernos
- NICs (tarjetas de red) actuales
- Equipos Ethernet **Gigabit y superiores** (en general)

> ⚠️ **Equipos antiguos** suelen **NO** soportar Auto MDI-X.

---

## 🧪 Ejemplos prácticos

| Conexión | Sin Auto MDI-X | Con Auto MDI-X |
|--------|---------------|---------------|
| PC ↔ PC | Crossover | Cualquier cable |
| Switch ↔ Switch | Crossover | Cualquier cable |
| Router ↔ Router | Crossover | Cualquier cable |
| PC ↔ Switch | Straight | Cualquier cable |

---

## 📌 Ventajas
- Simplifica instalaciones
- Reduce errores humanos
- Ahorra tiempo
- Evita problemas de conectividad física

---

## ❌ Limitaciones
- No existe en equipos viejos
- No corrige:
  - Cable defectuoso
  - Pines mal crimpados
  - Distancias mayores a 100 m
  - Problemas de capa 2 o superiores

---

## 🧠 Relación con el modelo OSI
- Pertenece a la **Capa 1 – Física**
- Actúa antes de que exista comunicación de datos real

---

## 📚 Clave para CCNA
- Si **NO hay Auto MDI-X**, debés elegir el cable correcto
- En escenarios de examen:
  - “Old devices” → **NO Auto MDI-X**
  - “Modern devices” → **Sí Auto MDI-X**

---

**Neighbor Discovery** es el conjunto de mecanismos que usa **IPv6** para que los dispositivos en la misma red local:
- Se encuentren entre sí
- Obtengan información de red
- Resuelvan direcciones IP ↔ MAC
- Detecten routers disponibles

Reemplaza funciones que en IPv4 hacían **ARP, ICMP Router Discovery y DHCP básico**.
## Para qué sirve
Neighbor Discovery permite:
1. **Autoconfiguración de direcciones (SLAAC)**  
    El host obtiene su dirección IPv6 automáticamente desde los anuncios del router.
2. **Resolución de direcciones**  
    Convierte una dirección IPv6 en dirección MAC (equivalente a ARP en IPv4).
3. **Detección de routers**  
    Encuentra el router por defecto en la red local. 4. **Detección de vecinos alcanzables**  
    Verifica si otro host sigue activo.
5. **Redirecciones**  
    El router puede indicar una mejor ruta dentro de la LAN.

## Mensajes ICMPv6 usados
Neighbor Discovery se basa en **ICMPv6**:
- **Router Solicitation (RS)** → el host pregunta por routers
- **Router Advertisement (RA)** → el router responde con configuración
- **Neighbor Solicitation (NS)** → consulta la MAC de un vecino o verifica alcance
- **Neighbor Advertisement (NA)** → respuesta con la MAC
- **Redirect** → indica una mejor ruta local
---
## Diferencias clave vs IPv4
- No usa **ARP** → todo está integrado en **ICMPv6**
- Permite **autoconfiguración sin DHCP**
- Diseñado para **seguridad y eficiencia multicast**
- Menos broadcast, más uso de **multicast específico**

En redes, el **payload** es la **información útil** que se quiere transportar, excluyendo los datos de control.

Cuando un mensaje baja por las capas del modelo OSI:
- Cada capa **agrega su propio header** (y a veces trailer).
- El contenido que recibe una capa superior se convierte en el **payload** de la capa inferior.

### Ejemplo
- **Payload de Capa 4 (TCP/UDP)**: datos de la aplicación (HTTP, DNS, etc.).
- **Payload de Capa 3 (IP)**: segmento TCP/UDP completo.
- **Payload de Capa 2 (Ethernet)**: paquete IP completo.

### Idea clave
> El payload es el dato que **una capa encapsula y transporta**, mientras que los headers y trailers sirven para control y entrega.

En resumen, el payload es “lo importante” del mensaje desde el punto de vista de cada capa.

## What is CCNA?
- **CCNA (Cisco Certified Network Associate)** is an entry-level networking certification.
- Validates knowledge in:
  - Network fundamentals
  - IP connectivity
  - Network access
  - Basic security
  - Automation and introduction to modern networks
- Ideal for:
  - Students
  - IT beginners
  - Individuals targeting roles such as **IT Support, Network Technician, Junior SysAdmin**

---

## What is a Network?
- A **network** is a collection of devices connected together to:
  - Share data
  - Share resources (internet, printers, servers)
- Everyday examples:
  - Home network
  - Corporate / enterprise network
  - The Internet (a network of networks)

---

### Host / End Device
- An end device that **sends or receives data**
- Examples: PC, Laptop, Smartphone, Server

### Switch
- Connects devices **within the same local area network (LAN)**
- Main function: Forward data to the correct device within the local network

### Router
- Connects **different networks together**
- Main function: Route traffic from one network to another (e.g., LAN ↔ Internet)

---

## Network Types

### LAN (Local Area Network)
- Local Area Network
- Examples: Home, Office, School
- High speed, small geographical area

### WAN (Wide Area Network)
- Wide Area Network
- Example: The Internet
- Connects multiple LANs across large geographical distances

  - **OSI Model** (7 layers)

# Introduction
Network protocols and reference models are foundational to ensuring that devices can communicate regardless of hardware vendor or underlying technology. **Protocols** are agreed-upon rule sets governing communication, while **reference models** provide a layered framework to understand how these rules operate across network functions.

The overarching goal is interoperability, enabling a source host to efficiently deliver messages to a destination host across shared media.

# Communication Fundamentals
Effective communication requires three primary components:
- **Message Source** (Sender)
- **Message Destination** (Receiver)
- **Channel** (Transmission Medium)

Communication is governed by protocols defining message format, timing, and transmission methods.

**Message Encoding**: Converting information into an acceptable physical format for transmission (electrical pulses, light waves, RF signals). The inverse process is **decoding**.

**Formatting and Encapsulation**: Structuring data according to media requirements (analogous to placing a letter into an addressed envelope).

# Protocol Requirements
- **Message Size**: Regulates the maximum data payload transmitted at once. Large data streams are segmented into smaller blocks.
- **Message Timing**:
  - **Flow Control**: Managing transmission rates to prevent overwhelming receivers.
  - **Response Timeout**: The duration a host waits for an acknowledgment before assuming packet loss.
  - **Access Method**: Determines when a station may transmit on a shared medium to prevent or handle collisions.
- **Delivery Options**:
  - **Unicast**: Delivery to a single, specific end device.
  - **Multicast**: Delivery to a designated group of interested devices.
  - **Broadcast**: Delivery to all devices on the local broadcast domain.

# Protocol Suites
A **protocol suite** is a set of interrelated protocols working together. They operate as a layered stack, where lower layers manage network transmission and upper layers handle application data.

The predominant protocol suite is **TCP/IP**, an open standard maintained by the **IETF**. It superseded proprietary stacks such as AppleTalk and Novell NetWare, guaranteeing multivendor hardware and software interoperability.

# Standards Organizations
Open standards foster innovation and competition, developed by vendor-neutral international organizations:
- **ISOC** (Internet Society), **IAB** (Internet Architecture Board), and **IETF** (Internet Engineering Task Force, which publishes RFCs).
- **ICANN** and **IANA**: Coordinate IP address space allocation and DNS root zones.
- **IEEE**: Defines physical and data link standards, including IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet) and IEEE 802.11 (WLAN/Wi-Fi).
- **TIA/EIA**: Develops cabling and wiring termination standards.

# Reference Models
Layered models modularize network functions, fostering compatibility and isolating layer changes.

### OSI Model
The **OSI Model** defines 7 numbered layers:
1. Physical
2. Data Link
3. Network
4. Transport
5. Session
6. Presentation
7. Application

![[Pasted image 20260124114015.png]]

### TCP/IP Model
The operational architecture of the global Internet, composed of 4 functional layers:
- 4. **Application**
- 3. **Transport**
- 2. **Internet**
- 1. **Network Access**

![[Pasted image 20260124114049.png]]
![[Pasted image 20260124114324.png]]

#### TCP/IP Suite Protocols by Layer

***Application Layer***
Provides services directly to end-user applications:
- **DNS (Domain Name System)**: Resolves human-readable domain names (e.g., cisco.com) to numeric IP addresses.
- **DHCP (v4 and v6)**: Dynamically leases IP configuration to client hosts.
- **SLAAC**: Stateless IPv6 address autoconfiguration using router advertisements.
- **SMTP**: Email transmission between mail transfer agents (MTAs).
- **POP3 / IMAP**: Protocols used by email clients to retrieve messages from a mail server.
- **FTP**: Reliable, connection-oriented client-server file transfers.
- **TFTP**: Lightweight, connectionless UDP-based file transfer.
- **SFTP**: Secure, SSH-encrypted file transfer.
- **HTTP / HTTPS**: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (cleartext / TLS-encrypted) powering the World Wide Web.
- **REST**: Architectural web service interface utilizing HTTP methods.

***Transport Layer***
Manages end-to-end process-to-process communication between hosts:
- **TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)**: Connection-oriented, reliable, sequenced, stateful byte-stream delivery with flow control and windowing.
- **UDP (User Datagram Protocol)**: Connectionless, lightweight, low-overhead datagram delivery without acknowledgments ("best-effort").

***Internet Layer***
Responsible for logical addressing, path determination, and packet routing:
- **IPv4**: 32-bit logical addressing scheme.
- **IPv6**: 128-bit hierarchical addressing scheme.
- **NAT (Network Address Translation)**: Translates private RFC 1918 addresses into globally routable public IPs.
- **ICMP (v4 and v6)**: Control messaging and error reporting.
- **OSPF**: Open-standard link-state Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP).
- **EIGRP**: Cisco advanced distance-vector routing protocol.
- **BGP**: Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) routing the global Internet backbone.

***Network Access Layer***
Manages physical network hardware, signaling, and data link frame exchange:
- **ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)**: Dynamically resolves a known IPv4 address into a Layer 2 MAC address.
- **Ethernet (IEEE 802.3)**: Defines wired LAN framing and signaling.
- **WLAN (IEEE 802.11)**: Defines wireless radio transmission framing.

# Data Encapsulation
**Encapsulation** adds protocol control headers (and trailers) as data moves down the stack from application to physical medium:
- **Data**: Application Layer
- **Segment / Datagram**: Transport Layer (adds source and destination port numbers)
- **Packet**: Network Layer (adds source and destination IP addresses)
- **Frame**: Data Link Layer (adds source and destination MAC addresses and Frame Check Sequence)
- **Bits**: Physical Layer (encoded signal transmission)

# OSI vs TCP/IP Comparison
| OSI Layer | TCP/IP Layer | PDU Name |
|-----------|--------------|----------|
| Application | Application | Data |
| Presentation | Application | Data |
| Session | Application | Data |
| Transport | Transport | Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP) |
| Network | Internet | Packet (IP) |
| Data Link | Network Access | Frame (Ethernet) |
| Physical | Network Access | Bits |

# Data Access and Addressing
- **IP Address (Layer 3 Logical Address)**: Identifies the original source and final destination host across routed internetworks.
- **MAC Address (Layer 2 Physical Address)**: Identifies the physical interface on the immediate local segment, rewritten on each router hop.

### Communication on the Same Local Subnet
When the source and destination reside within the same subnet, frames are delivered directly:
- **Source IP**: Local Host IP
- **Destination IP**: Local Target IP
- **Source MAC**: Local Host NIC MAC
- **Destination MAC**: Local Target NIC MAC (resolved via [[resources/ARP|ARP]])

### Communication on a Remote Network
When the destination host is outside the local network:
- **Source IP**: Host IP (e.g., 192.168.1.110)
- **Destination IP**: Remote Server IP (e.g., 172.16.1.99)
- **Source MAC**: Host NIC MAC
- **Destination MAC**: **Default Gateway (Router) Interface MAC**

The router strips the Layer 2 Ethernet frame, examines the destination Layer 3 IP address, performs a route table lookup, and encapsulates the packet into a new Layer 2 frame with the next-hop MAC address.

#### Lab Insights
When pinging a local device, the destination MAC address belongs directly to the target device (obtained via [[resources/ARP|ARP]]).
When pinging a URL/hostname, DNS resolution occurs first to obtain the destination IP address, and the frame is addressed to the default gateway's MAC address.

### Switch Virtual Interface (SVI)
```text

```
- A **logical (virtual) interface**, not tied to a single physical port.
- Provides an **IP address** on the switch.
- Used for **in-band remote management** (SSH, Telnet, SNMP, HTTPS).

When a Layer 2 switch is positioned between two communicating hosts, the frame's destination MAC is either the final host or the router gateway—**never the Layer 2 switch's MAC address**.

Introduction

Network protocols and reference models are foundational to ensuring that devices can communicate regardless of hardware vendor or underlying technology. Protocols are agreed-upon rule sets governing communication, while reference models provide a layered framework to understand how these rules operate across network functions.

The overarching goal is interoperability, enabling a source host to efficiently deliver messages to a destination host across shared media.

Communication Fundamentals

Effective communication requires three primary components:

  • Message Source (Sender)
  • Message Destination (Receiver)
  • Channel (Transmission Medium)

Communication is governed by protocols defining message format, timing, and transmission methods.

Message Encoding: Converting information into an acceptable physical format for transmission (electrical pulses, light waves, RF signals). The inverse process is decoding.

Formatting and Encapsulation: Structuring data according to media requirements (analogous to placing a letter into an addressed envelope).

Protocol Requirements

  • Message Size: Regulates the maximum data payload transmitted at once. Large data streams are segmented into smaller blocks.
  • Message Timing:
    • Flow Control: Managing transmission rates to prevent overwhelming receivers.
    • Response Timeout: The duration a host waits for an acknowledgment before assuming packet loss.
    • Access Method: Determines when a station may transmit on a shared medium to prevent or handle collisions.
  • Delivery Options:
    • Unicast: Delivery to a single, specific end device.
    • Multicast: Delivery to a designated group of interested devices.
    • Broadcast: Delivery to all devices on the local broadcast domain.

Protocol Suites

A protocol suite is a set of interrelated protocols working together. They operate as a layered stack, where lower layers manage network transmission and upper layers handle application data.

The predominant protocol suite is TCP/IP, an open standard maintained by the IETF. It superseded proprietary stacks such as AppleTalk and Novell NetWare, guaranteeing multivendor hardware and software interoperability.

Standards Organizations

Open standards foster innovation and competition, developed by vendor-neutral international organizations:

  • ISOC (Internet Society), IAB (Internet Architecture Board), and IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force, which publishes RFCs).
  • ICANN and IANA: Coordinate IP address space allocation and DNS root zones.
  • IEEE: Defines physical and data link standards, including IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet) and IEEE 802.11 (WLAN/Wi-Fi).
  • TIA/EIA: Develops cabling and wiring termination standards.

Reference Models

Layered models modularize network functions, fostering compatibility and isolating layer changes.

OSI Model

The OSI Model defines 7 numbered layers:

  1. Physical
  2. Data Link
  3. Network
  4. Transport
  5. Session
  6. Presentation
  7. Application

TCP/IP Model

The operational architecture of the global Internet, composed of 4 functional layers:

  • 4. Application
    1. Transport
    1. Internet
    1. Network Access

TCP/IP Suite Protocols by Layer

Application Layer Provides services directly to end-user applications:

  • DNS (Domain Name System): Resolves human-readable domain names (e.g., cisco.com) to numeric IP addresses.
  • DHCP (v4 and v6): Dynamically leases IP configuration to client hosts.
  • SLAAC: Stateless IPv6 address autoconfiguration using router advertisements.
  • SMTP: Email transmission between mail transfer agents (MTAs).
  • POP3 / IMAP: Protocols used by email clients to retrieve messages from a mail server.
  • FTP: Reliable, connection-oriented client-server file transfers.
  • TFTP: Lightweight, connectionless UDP-based file transfer.
  • SFTP: Secure, SSH-encrypted file transfer.
  • HTTP / HTTPS: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (cleartext / TLS-encrypted) powering the World Wide Web.
  • REST: Architectural web service interface utilizing HTTP methods.

Transport Layer Manages end-to-end process-to-process communication between hosts:

  • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Connection-oriented, reliable, sequenced, stateful byte-stream delivery with flow control and windowing.
  • UDP (User Datagram Protocol): Connectionless, lightweight, low-overhead datagram delivery without acknowledgments (“best-effort”).

Internet Layer Responsible for logical addressing, path determination, and packet routing:

  • IPv4: 32-bit logical addressing scheme.
  • IPv6: 128-bit hierarchical addressing scheme.
  • NAT (Network Address Translation): Translates private RFC 1918 addresses into globally routable public IPs.
  • ICMP (v4 and v6): Control messaging and error reporting.
  • OSPF: Open-standard link-state Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP).
  • EIGRP: Cisco advanced distance-vector routing protocol.
  • BGP: Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) routing the global Internet backbone.

Network Access Layer Manages physical network hardware, signaling, and data link frame exchange:

  • ARP (Address Resolution Protocol): Dynamically resolves a known IPv4 address into a Layer 2 MAC address.
  • Ethernet (IEEE 802.3): Defines wired LAN framing and signaling.
  • WLAN (IEEE 802.11): Defines wireless radio transmission framing.

Data Encapsulation

Encapsulation adds protocol control headers (and trailers) as data moves down the stack from application to physical medium:

  • Data: Application Layer
  • Segment / Datagram: Transport Layer (adds source and destination port numbers)
  • Packet: Network Layer (adds source and destination IP addresses)
  • Frame: Data Link Layer (adds source and destination MAC addresses and Frame Check Sequence)
  • Bits: Physical Layer (encoded signal transmission)

## 1. What is the Cisco IOS CLI?

The Cisco IOS *Command-Line Interface* (CLI) is the primary method to interact with Cisco routers and switches to **configure, monitor, and troubleshoot the device**. It enables operators to directly execute commands, inspect interface states, and alter operational settings.

#### Methods of Accessing the CLI
Before using the CLI, you must **connect to the device**:
- **Physical Console Port**: Using a rollover cable connected to the console RJ-45 or mini-USB port.
- **SSH (Secure Shell)**: Encrypted remote CLI management access.
- **Telnet**: Legacy unencrypted remote access (insecure, sends credentials in cleartext).

#### Command Mode Hierarchy
##### User EXEC Mode:
- Initial prompt upon login.
- Allows **basic informational and troubleshooting commands** like `show`, `ping`, and `traceroute`.
- Typical prompt: `Router>`
- Does not allow altering configuration.

##### Privileged EXEC Mode:
- Administrative / privileged access level.
- Accessed from User EXEC using the command:
  `enable`
- Typical prompt: `Router#`
- Allows viewing detailed operational data (`show running-config`), managing device storage, and issuing reboot commands.
- Commands here do not alter device configuration directly; they inspect or manage state.

##### Global Configuration Mode:
- Used to **make global changes to the system configuration**.
- Accessed from Privileged EXEC:
  `configure terminal`
- Typical prompt: `Router(config)#`
- Commands applied here affect the entire device globally.

##### Sub-configuration Modes (Interface, Line, Routing, etc.)
From Global Configuration, you enter specific sub-modes:
- **Interface Configuration**: Configure physical or logical interfaces (`Router(config-if)#`).
- **Line Configuration**: Configure console, auxiliary, or VTY/remote access lines (`Router(config-line)#`).
- **Routing Protocol Configuration**: Configure OSPF, EIGRP, etc. (`Router(config-router)#`).
- **Access-List Configuration**: Configure security filtering lists (`Router(config-ext-nacl)#`).

Example entering interface configuration:
`interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1`  
Prompt: `Router(config-if)#`

##### Other Modes
- **Setup Mode**: Guided initial setup dialog prompt upon booting without a configuration.
- **ROM Monitor (ROMMON)**: Low-level diagnostic and recovery environment used when IOS cannot boot normally.

## CLI Help and Navigation
- Type `?` to **display available commands** in the current mode or check parameter syntax:
  `Router#?`  
  `Router#show ?`
- Auto-complete commands using the **TAB** key.

# Common Foundational Commands
- `show version`: Displays Cisco IOS version, hardware details, uptime, and configuration register.
- `show running-config`: Displays the active configuration in RAM.
- `show startup-config`: Displays the saved configuration in NVRAM.

### Saving Configuration
- `copy running-config startup-config` (or shorthand `copy run start`): Writes the running configuration from RAM into NVRAM so changes persist after a reboot.

### Mode Navigation
- `exit`: Drops back one level in the command hierarchy.
- `end` or `Ctrl + Z`: Returns immediately to Privileged EXEC (`Router#`).

## Privilege Levels and Security
- Commands are tied to **privilege levels** (0 to 15, where 15 is full root administrative access). Higher levels require proper authentication.

## Additional Key Concepts
### a. Pipe and Output Filtering
Filter CLI output from `show` commands using pipes:
- `show running-config | include interface`
- `show running-config | section line`
- `show running-config | begin router`

# Lab Commands Reference:

- `Ctrl + Shift + 6`: Universal Cisco break sequence (aborts pings, traceroutes, DNS lookups).
- `enable`: Enter Privileged EXEC mode.
- `configure terminal`: Enter Global Configuration mode.
- `hostname R1`: Set device hostname.
- `enable password CCNA`: Set plaintext Privileged EXEC password (weak).
- `service password-encryption`: Encrypt plaintext passwords (uses Type 7 weak reversible cipher).
- `enable secret Cisco`: Set securely hashed Privileged EXEC secret (Type 5/Type 8/Type 9).

> If both `enable secret` and `enable password` are configured, `enable secret` takes precedence and is used.

- `do <command>`: Execute Privileged EXEC commands from within Global Configuration or sub-modes (e.g. `do show ip route`).
- `copy running-config startup-config`: Save changes to NVRAM.

# Useful Operational Commands
- `banner motd "Authorized Access Only!"`: Configure Message of the Day login banner.
- `show running-config`: View active running configuration.
- `show ip interface brief`: Overview of all interfaces, assigned IP addresses, and layer 1/layer 2 status.
- `line console 0`: Select physical console port for security configuration.

# Configuration Walkthrough: Securing Device Access

### Secure Access to the Console Line
```text
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# line console 0
S1(config-line)# password letmein
S1(config-line)# login
S1(config-line)# exit
```

### Secure Privileged EXEC Mode
```text
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# enable password c1$c0
S1(config)# exit
```

### Encrypt Plaintext Passwords
```text
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# service password-encryption
S1(config)# exit
```

### Configure Enable Secret
```text
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# enable secret itsasecret
S1(config)# exit
```

### Save Configuration to NVRAM
```text
S1# copy running-config startup-config
Destination filename [startup-config]? [Enter]
Building configuration...
[OK]
```

## Configuring Management IP on a Switch (SVI)
Switches forward Layer 2 frames out-of-the-box using MAC addresses without requiring an IP address. An IP address is assigned to a Switch Virtual Interface (SVI) purely for remote management (SSH/Telnet/SNMP):

```text
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# interface vlan 1
S1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.253 255.255.255.0
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
S1(config-if)# exit
S1(config)# ip default-gateway 192.168.1.1
S1(config)# exit
```

### Protocols and Standards
- A **protocol** is an agreed-upon set of rules defining how data is formatted and transmitted between devices across a network.
  - Proprietary protocols created for a specific manufacturer's hardware hindered multi-vendor interoperability.
- A **standard** is an open, consensus-driven specification describing how a protocol or technology should function.
  - Vendor-neutral standards ensure that any compliant hardware or software can communicate seamlessly.

--- 

#### TCP/IP Model Overview
![[Pasted image 20260109175245.png]]
![[Pasted image 20260109175655.png]]

#### Layer 1: Physical Layer
- Transmits and receives raw bitstreams as electrical voltages, optical pulses, or radio waves across physical transmission media.
- Specifies physical components: cables, pinouts, transceivers, signaling levels, and transmission bit rates.
- Examples:
  - UTP copper cabling
  - Fiber-optic cabling
  - Wi-Fi radio frequencies and antennas

#### Layer 2: Data Link / Network Access Layer
- Provides hop-to-hop frame delivery within a local network segment (switches do not count as hops; they merely extend the local broadcast domain).
- Employs Media Access Control (**MAC**) addresses to identify network interfaces on the local segment.
- Core protocols:
  - Ethernet (IEEE 802.3)
  - Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11)

#### Layer 3: Internet Layer
- Provides end-to-end packet delivery between hosts across multiple interconnected networks.
- Uses logical **IP addresses** to identify hosts globally.
- Routers operate primarily at this layer, performing routing table lookups to forward packets toward the final destination host.
- Core protocols:
  - IPv4, IPv6
  - ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol)

#### Layer 4: Transport Layer
- Provides process-to-process communication sessions between applications.
- Uses **port numbers** (0–65535) to identify specific application processes running on hosts.
- Operates primarily on communicating end hosts rather than network intermediate devices.
- Core protocols:
  - **TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)**: Reliable, connection-oriented, sequenced.
  - **UDP (User Datagram Protocol)**: Lightweight, connectionless, unacknowledged.

#### Layer 5: Application Layer
- Interface where network communication meets user applications and operating system processes.
- Defines message formatting, syntax, and semantics for exchanging application data.
- Core protocols:
  - HTTP / HTTPS
  - FTP, TFTP
  - SMTP, POP3, IMAP
  - DNS, DHCP
- Intermediate infrastructure devices (routers, switches) generally ignore application layer contents; they simply forward the underlying payload.

## Encapsulation and De-encapsulation

### Encapsulation
- The application layer generates and formats data to transmit across the network.
- As the data descends through the protocol stack, each layer prepends a protocol header containing control metadata:
  - Source and destination addresses (port numbers at L4, IP addresses at L3, MAC addresses at L2).
  - Layer 2 additionally appends a trailer containing a Frame Check Sequence (FCS/CRC) to detect transmission errors.
- The physical layer encodes the resulting frame into physical signals transmitted across the medium.

![[Pasted image 20260109181541.png]]

### De-encapsulation
- The receiving host senses signals on the physical medium at Layer 1 and reconstructs the bitstream.
- Layer 2 validates the frame checksum (FCS). If valid and addressed to the host (or broadcast/multicast), the Layer 2 header and trailer are stripped.
- The Layer 3 engine parses the IP header, verifies the destination address, and removes the L3 header.
- The Layer 4 engine inspects the destination port, handles sequencing/reassembly, strips the L4 header, and directs the data to the matching application process.
- The application processes the data and prepares an optional response.

![[Pasted image 20260109182134.png]]

### Protocol Data Units (PDUs)
At each stage of encapsulation and de-encapsulation, the data package carries a specific designation:
- **Segment**: Layer 4 PDU for TCP (or **Datagram** for UDP).
- **Packet**: Layer 3 PDU (IP header + L4 payload).
- **Frame**: Layer 2 PDU (Ethernet header + L3 payload + FCS trailer).

![[Pasted image 20260109182557.png]]

Formally referenced by layer number:
- **L4PDU**: Segment / Datagram
- **L3PDU**: Packet
- **L2PDU**: Frame

The underlying data payload contained within any given PDU is called the [[resources/payload|payload]] (excluding current-layer header and trailer).

### Adjacent-Layer and Same-Layer Interactions
- **Adjacent-layer interaction**: Each layer provides services to the layer immediately above it and consumes services from the layer directly beneath it.
- **Same-layer interaction**: Each layer communicates logically with its peer layer on the remote communicating host using standardized protocol headers.

![[Pasted image 20260109183150.png]]

Encapsulation

  • The application layer generates and formats data to transmit across the network.
  • As the data descends through the protocol stack, each layer prepends a protocol header containing control metadata:
    • Source and destination addresses (port numbers at L4, IP addresses at L3, MAC addresses at L2).
    • Layer 2 additionally appends a trailer containing a Frame Check Sequence (FCS/CRC) to detect transmission errors.
  • The physical layer encodes the resulting frame into physical signals transmitted across the medium.

De-encapsulation

  • The receiving host senses signals on the physical medium at Layer 1 and reconstructs the bitstream.
  • Layer 2 validates the frame checksum (FCS). If valid and addressed to the host (or broadcast/multicast), the Layer 2 header and trailer are stripped.
  • The Layer 3 engine parses the IP header, verifies the destination address, and removes the L3 header.
  • The Layer 4 engine inspects the destination port, handles sequencing/reassembly, strips the L4 header, and directs the data to the matching application process.
  • The application processes the data and prepares an optional response.

Protocol Data Units (PDUs)

At each stage of encapsulation and de-encapsulation, the data package carries a specific designation:

  • Segment: Layer 4 PDU for TCP (or Datagram for UDP).
  • Packet: Layer 3 PDU (IP header + L4 payload).
  • Frame: Layer 2 PDU (Ethernet header + L3 payload + FCS trailer).

Formally referenced by layer number:

  • L4PDU: Segment / Datagram
  • L3PDU: Packet
  • L2PDU: Frame

The underlying data payload contained within any given PDU is called the payload (excluding current-layer header and trailer).

Adjacent-Layer and Same-Layer Interactions

  • Adjacent-layer interaction: Each layer provides services to the layer immediately above it and consumes services from the layer directly beneath it.
  • Same-layer interaction: Each layer communicates logically with its peer layer on the remote communicating host using standardized protocol headers.

The OSI Model
  • Created by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as a 7-layer theoretical reference framework.
  • Although proprietary OSI protocol implementations were ultimately eclipsed by the practical adoption of TCP/IP, the 7-layer terminology remains the universal industry standard for teaching and network troubleshooting.

# Physical Layer
The Physical Layer of the OSI Model (or Network Access layer of [[3.1 TCP-IP]]) provides the electrical, optical, and mechanical means to transport the raw bits that constitute a Data Link frame across network media. It accepts a complete frame from the Data Link layer and encodes it as a continuous series of physical signals.

![[Pasted image 20260127072048.png]]

### Physical Layer Standards Organizations
- **ISO** (International Organization for Standardization)
- **TIA/EIA** (Telecommunications Industry Association / Electronic Industries Alliance)
- **ITU** (International Telecommunication Union)
- **ANSI** (American National Standards Institute)
- **IEEE** (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)
- National regulatory bodies (FCC in the USA, ETSI in Europe)
- Regional cabling standards: CSA (Canada), CENELEC (Europe), JSA/JIS (Japan).

Physical layer standards govern three functional areas:
1. **Physical Components**: Connectors, jacks, pinouts, transceivers, cable shielding, and hardware specifications.
2. **Encoding**: Converting a stream of raw data bits into a standardized transmission code pattern recognizable by transmitter and receiver.
   - For example, **Manchester encoding** (used in legacy 10 Mbps 10BASE-T) represents a bit 0 with a high-to-low voltage transition, and a bit 1 with a low-to-high transition in the middle of the bit interval.
   - Higher data rates employ more advanced line encoding schemes: 100BASE-TX uses 4B/5B encoding, while 1000BASE-T employs 8B/10B or PAM-5.
   ![[Pasted image 20260127073928.png]]
3. **Signaling**: How bits are physically modulated onto the medium.
   - Voltage levels on copper wire:
   ![[Pasted image 20260127074102.png]]
   - Pulses of light through fiber-optic strands:
   ![[Pasted image 20260127074115.png]]
   - Radio frequency modulations transmitted wirelessly:
   ![[Pasted image 20260127074201.png]]

### Bandwidth
Bandwidth measures the maximum capacity of a physical medium to carry data over time. Digital bandwidth measures how many bits can flow from one point to another in a given time interval.
In both 10 Mbps and 100 Mbps Ethernet, electrical signals travel across copper at roughly the speed of electricity; the difference lies in the density and frequency of bits transmitted per second.

| Unit of Bandwidth | Abbreviation | Equivalence in bps |
|-------------------|--------------|---------------------|
| Bits per second | bps | 1 bps (fundamental unit) |
| Kilobits per second | kbps | $1,000\text{ bps} = 10^3\text{ bps}$ |
| Megabits per second | Mbps | $1,000,000\text{ bps} = 10^6\text{ bps}$ |
| Gigabits per second | Gbps | $1,000,000,000\text{ bps} = 10^9\text{ bps}$ |
| Terabits per second | Tbps | $1,000,000,000,000\text{ bps} = 10^{12}\text{ bps}$ |

#### Bandwidth Terminology
- **Latency**: The elapsed time (including queueing and serialization delays) for data to traverse from source to destination. Across an internetwork, end-to-end throughput is bottlenecked by the slowest link along the transmission path.
- **Throughput**: The actual volume of bits successfully transferred across a medium within a given time period. In real-world networks, throughput is lower than theoretical bandwidth due to network congestion, protocol overhead, and latency.
- **Goodput**: The measure of usable application data transferred per unit time:
  $$\text{Goodput} = \text{Throughput} - \text{Protocol Overhead (Headers, Handshakes, ACKs, Retransmissions)}$$
  $$\text{Goodput} < \text{Throughput} \le \text{Bandwidth}$$

- **BASE**: Baseband signaling (the entire channel bandwidth carries a single signal).
- **T**: Twisted-pair copper wiring.
Ethernet over copper uses [[resources/UTP cable|UTP cables]].

## Copper Cabling
Inexpensive, easy to install, and low electrical resistance, but bounded by distance limits and signal degradation (attenuation).
Susceptible to two major forms of noise:
- **EMI (Electromagnetic Interference) and RFI (Radio Frequency Interference)**: Distorts signals; generated by motors, fluorescent ballasts, power lines, and radio transmitters.
- **Crosstalk**: Unwanted coupling of magnetic/electrical fields from one wire pair into an adjacent wire pair.

Mitigation:
- Shielding (foil/braid) grounded properly.
- Twisting wire pairs together: Current flowing in opposite directions in each wire of a circuit produces complementary opposing magnetic fields that cancel each other out (cancellation effect).

### Types of Copper Cables
1. **[[resources/UTP cable|UTP (Unshielded Twisted-Pair)]]**: Most common LAN media; terminated with RJ-45 modular connectors. 4 color-coded twisted pairs enclosed in a flexible jacket.
   ![[Pasted image 20260127082910.png]]
2. **STP (Shielded Twisted-Pair)**: Better EMI/RFI immunity and crosstalk reduction than UTP, but significantly more expensive, thicker, and harder to terminate. Requires proper electrical grounding.
   ![[Pasted image 20260127083401.png]]
3. **Coaxial Cable**: Two concentric conductors sharing a common physical axis (center copper core, dielectric insulator, woven copper braid shield, outer jacket). Terminated using BNC, F-type, or N-type connectors.
   - Still used for connecting wireless antennas and in DOCSIS cable internet services.

## UTP Cabling Standards
Defined by TIA/EIA-568:
- Category 5: 100 Mbps (100BASE-TX)
- Category 5e: 1,000 Mbps / 1 Gbps (1000BASE-T) — minimum acceptable standard today
- Category 6: 1 Gbps up to 100 m, 10 Gbps up to 55 m
- Category 6a: 10 Gbps up to full 100 m
- Category 7 / 8: High-frequency data center runs up to 40 Gbps
![[Pasted image 20260127090803.png]]

### Straight-Through vs Crossover Pinouts
- **Straight-Through**: Connects unlike devices (PC to Switch, Switch to Router).
- **Crossover**: Connects like devices (Switch to Switch, PC to PC, Router to Router).
- **Rollover (Console)**: Proprietary Cisco pinout used to connect a workstation COM/USB port to a console management port.
- Modern devices use **[[resources/auto MDI-X|auto MDI-X]]** to detect and automatically cross pin connections internally.
![[Pasted image 20260127091321.png]]
![[Pasted image 20260127091327.png]]

## Fiber-Optic Cabling
Employs modular [[resources/SFP|SFP]] transceivers on switch and router uplinks. Optical cables utilize two strands (one transmit, one receive) or single-strand BiDi.

![[Pasted image 20260104141606.png]]

- Larger core diameter (50–62.5 microns).

  ![[Pasted image 20260127091859.png]]

## Comparison: UTP vs Fiber Optic

| Attribute | UTP Copper | Fiber Optic |
|-----------|------------|-------------|
| **Cost** | Low cost media and terminations | Higher material and transceiver cost |
| **Distance** | 100 meters maximum channel limit | Kilometers to tens of kilometers |
| **EMI / RFI Immunity** | Vulnerable to external interference | Completely immune to electromagnetic noise |
| **Interface Hardware** | Inexpensive RJ-45 jacks | Modular [[resources/SFP|SFP / SFP+]] transceivers |
| **Security** | Emits slight electromagnetic radiation | Completely tap-proof against standard interception |

## Wireless Media
Transports electromagnetic radio frequency (RF) signals:
- **Coverage**: Obstacles, wall materials, and terrain attenuate RF energy.
- **Interference**: Competing RF sources (microwaves, cordless phones, neighboring Wi-Fi channels).
- **Security**: Open transmission medium requires strong WPA2/WPA3 enterprise encryption.
- **Shared Medium**: Wi-Fi operates in half-duplex using [[resources/CSMA-CA|CSMA/CA]]; client contention divides effective per-station bandwidth.

### Wireless Standards
- **Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11)**: Wireless LAN technology utilizing CSMA/CA.
- **Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15)**: WPAN device pairing up to 10–100 m.
- **Zigbee (IEEE 802.15.4)**: Low-power, low-bandwidth mesh protocol for IoT smart home sensors.
- **WiMAX (IEEE 802.16)**: Wireless broadband access.

## Lab & Exam Review Points
- `show ip interface brief`: Verifies interface assignments and link statuses.
- Serial cable clocking: **DCE** cables provide the clock rate signal to synchronizing **DTE** interfaces.
- **Point of Presence (POP)**: The access point where an ISP provides customer demarcation and upstream connectivity.
- **Media Access Control (MAC) determinants**:
  1. How nodes share the physical media (contention vs scheduled).
  2. How the topology appears logically to the Data Link Layer (point-to-point vs shared multi-access).
- **Hub-and-spoke WAN topology**: Multiple remote spoke branches connect directly to a centralized corporate hub rather than directly to each other.

# Identifying IPv4 Address Classes
The **first octet** (the first decimal value between 0 and 255) identifies the IPv4 class:

Reserved address ranges (cannot be assigned to host interfaces):
- `0.0.0.0 – 0.255.255.255`: Local network identifier / unassigned
- `127.0.0.0 – 127.255.255.255`: Loopback diagnostics testing

## Class A
- First octet range: **1 – 126**
- Default mask: `/8` (`255.0.0.0`)
- Designed for very large networks (16 million hosts per network).

## Class B
- First octet range: **128 – 191**
- Default mask: `/16` (`255.255.0.0`)
- Designed for medium to large networks (65,534 hosts per network).

## Class C
- First octet range: **192 – 223**
- Default mask: `/24` (`255.255.255.0`)
- Designed for small networks (254 hosts per network).

## Class D (Multicast)
- First octet range: **224 – 239**
- Reserved for multicast group addressing (no host unicast assignment).

## Class E (Experimental)
- First octet range: **240 – 254**
- Reserved for experimental and research purposes.

# Classful vs CIDR Default Masks
- **Class A**: `/8` (`255.0.0.0`) -> Range: 1–126
- **Class B**: `/16` (`255.255.0.0`) -> Range: 128–191
- **Class C**: `/24` (`255.255.255.0`) -> Range: 192–223
- **Class D**: Multicast (224–239)
- **Class E**: Experimental (240–254)

# Data Link Layer Overview
Prepares network data for physical transmission. Responsible for Network Interface Card (NIC) communications across the physical network media.
- Allows upper protocol layers to access the media without concern for physical wiring details.
- Accepts Layer 3 data packets (IPv4 or IPv6) and encapsulates them into Layer 2 frames.
- Controls how data is placed and received on the media (Media Access Control).
- Exchanges frames between endpoints across local network media.
- De-encapsulates received frames and routes the Layer 3 payload to the proper upper-layer protocol.
- Performs error detection, rejecting corrupted frames using frame check sequences.

The Data Link layer prepends Layer 2 source and destination addresses (such as MAC addresses) and appends a trailer containing error-detection data.

## IEEE 802.2 LAN/MAN Sublayers
The IEEE 802 LAN/MAN standard divides the Data Link Layer into two distinct sublayers:
1. **Logical Link Control (LLC)**: Defined by IEEE 802.2. Communicates between network software in the upper layers and hardware in the lower layers. Places protocol identification tags in the frame header to indicate which Layer 3 protocol (IPv4, IPv6) is carried inside.
2. **Media Access Control (MAC)**: Implemented in hardware (IEEE 802.3 Ethernet, IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi, IEEE 802.15 WPAN). Controls the physical NIC and handles:
   - **Data Encapsulation**:
     - Frame delimiting (preamble and start-of-frame flags for synchronization).
     - Physical addressing (source and destination MAC addresses).
     - Error detection (CRC/FCS in trailer).
   - **Media Access Control**: Regulates access to shared media and handles contention.

![[Pasted image 20260202195650.png]]

## Accessing the Medium
At each hop along a path across an internetwork, routers perform the following steps:
1. Accept the incoming frame from the physical medium.
2. De-encapsulate the frame, stripping the Layer 2 header and trailer.
3. Examine the destination IP address in the Layer 3 packet header to determine the best outgoing path.
4. Re-encapsulate the packet into a brand-new Layer 2 frame appropriate for the next segment's medium.
5. Transmit the new frame out the outgoing interface onto the physical medium.

# Network Topologies
The topology of a network defines the physical and logical arrangement of connected nodes:
- **Physical Topology**: Identifies actual physical connections, cable layouts, and hardware locations. Usually point-to-point (P2P) or star/extended-star.
- **Logical Topology**: Describes the virtual path and transmission mechanism frames follow to move between nodes, referencing IP addressing and interface configurations.

### WAN Topologies
#### Point-to-Point (P2P)
Consists of a direct, permanent link between two communicating endpoints.
![[Pasted image 20260203153512.png]]

#### Hub-and-Spoke
The WAN equivalent of a star topology: a centralized hub site interconnects multiple branch spoke sites via point-to-point circuits. Spokes cannot exchange traffic directly without traversing the central hub.
![[Pasted image 20260203153629.png]]

#### Mesh
Provides high availability by interconnecting all nodes directly to one another. Full mesh is costly and complex; organizations frequently employ **partial mesh** where only critical core sites have redundant interconnects.
![[Pasted image 20260203153747.png]]

### Point-to-Point WAN Characteristics
Frames placed on one end of a P2P link can only emerge at the opposite end.
**No MAC addresses are required in Point-to-Point WAN protocols (like PPP or HDLC)** because there are no competing hosts on the shared link.
![[Pasted image 20260203154116.png]]

### LAN Topologies

## Half-Duplex vs Full-Duplex
- **Half-Duplex**: Both devices can transmit and receive, but only one direction at a time (e.g., WLANs, legacy Ethernet hubs).
- **Full-Duplex**: Both devices transmit and receive simultaneously without collision risk (modern Ethernet switches with point-to-point dedicated microsegments).

# Media Access Control Methods
1. **Contention-Based Access**:
   Nodes compete for access in half-duplex mode.
   - **[[resources/CSMA-CD|CSMA/CD]]**: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (legacy bus / hub Ethernet).
   - **[[resources/CSMA-CA|CSMA/CA]]**: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (IEEE 802.11 WLANs).
2. **Controlled Access (Deterministic)**:
   Nodes take turns in sequence (e.g. Token Ring token passing). Inefficient under modern traffic demands.
   ![[Pasted image 20260203170259.png]]

## Collision Mitigation: CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA
- **CSMA/CD**: Devices listen before transmitting; if a simultaneous transmission produces a voltage collision, transmission halts, a jamming signal is sent, and a random exponential backoff countdown begins.
- **CSMA/CA**: In wireless environments where stations cannot detect simultaneous collisions while transmitting, stations declare transmission duration windows and wait for random backoff intervals before transmitting, requiring explicit ACK confirmations.

# Data Link Frame Structure
Every Layer 2 frame consists of three primary components:
1. **Header**: Contains addressing, frame delimiters, and type identifiers.
2. **Data / Payload**: Layer 3 packet.
3. **Trailer**: Frame Check Sequence (FCS / CRC) for error detection.

![[Pasted image 20260203190400.png]]

### Frame Fields
- **Frame Start / Stop Indicators**: Synchronization flags marking frame boundaries.
- **Addressing**: Source and destination MAC addresses on the local medium.
- **Type / Length**: Identifies the encapsulated Layer 3 protocol (e.g., `0x0800` for IPv4, `0x86DD` for IPv6).
- **Control**: Flow control and QoS priority markers.
- **Data**: Layer 3 packet [[resources/payload|payload]].
- **Error Detection (FCS)**: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) calculated by the sender and verified by the receiver to detect bit corruption.

# Layer 2 Address Progression Across Routers
- **Host to Router**: Source MAC is PC; Destination MAC is Router Default Gateway.
  ![[Pasted image 20260203192906.png]]
- **Router to Router**: Router 1 de-encapsulates the frame, consults routing tables, and creates a new frame where Source MAC is R1's outgoing interface and Destination MAC is R2's interface.
  ![[Pasted image 20260203193101.png]]
- **Router to Destination Host**: Router 2 creates a new frame where Source MAC is R2's local interface and Destination MAC is the final target server's MAC address.
  ![[Pasted image 20260203193653.png]]

> **Lab Tip**: After de-encapsulating a received frame, the first thing a router does is examine the destination IP address and **determine the best path** using its routing table before re-encapsulating.

Data Link Layer Overview

Prepares network data for physical transmission. Responsible for Network Interface Card (NIC) communications across the physical network media.

  • Allows upper protocol layers to access the media without concern for physical wiring details.
  • Accepts Layer 3 data packets (IPv4 or IPv6) and encapsulates them into Layer 2 frames.
  • Controls how data is placed and received on the media (Media Access Control).
  • Exchanges frames between endpoints across local network media.
  • De-encapsulates received frames and routes the Layer 3 payload to the proper upper-layer protocol.
  • Performs error detection, rejecting corrupted frames using frame check sequences.

The Data Link layer prepends Layer 2 source and destination addresses (such as MAC addresses) and appends a trailer containing error-detection data.

IEEE 802.2 LAN/MAN Sublayers

The IEEE 802 LAN/MAN standard divides the Data Link Layer into two distinct sublayers:

  1. Logical Link Control (LLC): Defined by IEEE 802.2. Communicates between network software in the upper layers and hardware in the lower layers. Places protocol identification tags in the frame header to indicate which Layer 3 protocol (IPv4, IPv6) is carried inside.
  2. Media Access Control (MAC): Implemented in hardware (IEEE 802.3 Ethernet, IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi, IEEE 802.15 WPAN). Controls the physical NIC and handles:
    • Data Encapsulation:
      • Frame delimiting (preamble and start-of-frame flags for synchronization).
      • Physical addressing (source and destination MAC addresses).
      • Error detection (CRC/FCS in trailer).
    • Media Access Control: Regulates access to shared media and handles contention.

Accessing the Medium

At each hop along a path across an internetwork, routers perform the following steps:

  1. Accept the incoming frame from the physical medium.
  2. De-encapsulate the frame, stripping the Layer 2 header and trailer.
  3. Examine the destination IP address in the Layer 3 packet header to determine the best outgoing path.
  4. Re-encapsulate the packet into a brand-new Layer 2 frame appropriate for the next segment’s medium.
  5. Transmit the new frame out the outgoing interface onto the physical medium.

Consists of a direct, permanent link between two communicating endpoints.

Hub-and-Spoke

The WAN equivalent of a star topology: a centralized hub site interconnects multiple branch spoke sites via point-to-point circuits. Spokes cannot exchange traffic directly without traversing the central hub.
